titolo: How Ordinary Families Made a Dollar Last a Week During the Great Depression
descrizione: How did ordinary American families stretch every dollar during the Great Depression? This warm look at 1930s home life covers cheap food, home canning, feed sack clothing, mending, neighbors, and the New Deal. Learn how people cooked, patched, traded, and saved when money was scarce.

scene.testo: Millions of families lived on almost no cash in the 1930s.
Yet most of them still ate every single day.
They did it with tricks you have probably never heard.
Some of those tricks sound strange today.
Some of them were honestly pure genius.
Stay to the end, and you'll see how it worked.
But the biggest money-saver was not a recipe at all.
It was something nobody could buy in a store.
I'll reveal it near the end.
First, let's step into the kitchen of 1932.
The Great Depression began with the stock market crash of 1929.
But the crash was only the start.
Over the next years, thousands of banks closed their doors.
Families who trusted those banks lost their savings.
Businesses cut wages, cut hours, or shut down entirely.
By 1933, about one in four workers had no job.
That was the worst point of the whole decade.
No one in a family could count on a paycheck.
So every household turned into a tiny, careful economy.
And the first place they watched was the grocery bill.
Food took a huge share of a working family's income.
So cooks leaned on cheap, filling foods that lasted.
Dried beans were a pantry hero.
They cost little, and one pot fed everyone.
Potatoes, cornmeal, flour, and rice did the same job.
Cornmeal mush could be eaten hot for breakfast.
Then leftover mush was sliced and fried for supper.
Nothing was thrown out if it could still be eaten.
Meat was no longer the center of the plate.
A little went a long way in a stew.
Cooks stretched ground meat with oats, bread crumbs, or rice.
Cheaper cuts simmered for hours until they turned tender.
Gravy over bread made a meal out of almost nothing.
Bread itself was often baked at home.
Store loaves cost money, but flour went further.
Sliced bread was new, having first appeared in 1928.
Many homes still sliced their own loaves by hand.
Stale bread was never wasted in a careful home.
It became pudding, stuffing, toast, or crumbs for coating.
But that's not the strangest part.
Some families baked cakes with no eggs, milk, or butter.
Those were scarce or costly, so recipes adapted.
People later called them Depression cakes.
Dessert still mattered, even when money did not.
A birthday needed some kind of sweetness.
Then, in 1937, a new boxed dinner arrived.
Kraft Macaroni and Cheese was cheap and easy to store.
The company advertised it as a meal for a family.
That same year, Hormel introduced a canned meat called Spam.
Canned foods made shopping simpler for busy households.
But the cheapest food was the food you grew.
Families dug up backyards and empty lots for vegetables.
Tomatoes, beans, cabbage, and squash filled the rows.
Farm families also kept cows, hogs, and chickens.
Even some town families kept a few hens.
Eggs gave them protein without a trip to the store.
Children weeded, hauled water, and chased off the pests.
Garden work was a daily part of life.
In some places, people also gathered wild greens.
Dandelion leaves went into the pot for free.
When summer ended, the real work of saving began.
Women spent hot afternoons canning vegetables and fruit.
Jars were filled, sealed, and lined up in cellars.
A full shelf meant a family could face winter.
Extra jars were traded with neighbors.
Some people dried apples and beans to keep them.
Others stored potatoes and root vegetables in cool cellars.
Salt, smoke, and cold storage kept meat from spoiling.
Farm families often butchered a hog in the cold months.
Every part of the animal had a use.
Now think about clothing, another quiet drain on money.
The rule was simple: make it last.
An old saying went: use it up, wear it out.
Make it do, or do without.
Mothers patched knees and darned socks by lamplight.
Collars were turned so the frayed side hid underneath.
Coats were passed down from child to child.
A big brother's shirt became a little brother's shirt.
When cloth finally gave out, it was not thrown away.
It was cut up and sewn into quilts.
Then came one of the cleverest tricks of the era.
Flour and feed often came in cotton sacks.
Women washed those sacks and sewed them into clothes.
Soon the mills noticed what shoppers were doing.
They began printing flowers and patterns on the cloth.
A farm wife could choose flour by the design.
One sack might become an apron or a child's dress.
Several matching sacks could make a whole shirt.
Pillowcases and curtains came from the same cloth.
Even the bag was part of the bargain.
Shoes were another worry, especially with growing children.
A cobbler could resole a pair for far less than new.
When a sole wore through, some used cardboard inside.
Children saved their good shoes for church and school.
In summer, many went barefoot to spare the leather.
Inside the home, the same thinking ruled.
Broken chairs were glued, nailed, and tied back together.
Worn sheets were cut down the middle and flipped.
The thin center was sewn to the outside edges.
Old towels became rags, and rags became rugs.
Heating the house took money too, so families economized.
Many closed off rooms and lived around one stove.
Coal, wood, or even corncobs fed the fire.
Bedrooms stayed cold, so heavy quilts piled on the beds.
Children dressed fast beside the warm kitchen stove.
Electric lights were switched off the moment a room emptied.
Wash day meant hauling water and scrubbing by hand.
Clothes dried on a line, even in winter cold.
Homemade soap was made from saved kitchen fat.
Fat from cooking was never poured down the drain.
Yet life was not all work and worry.
Families still found ways to laugh together.
The radio became the center of many living rooms.
Families gathered to hear music, comedy, and news.
In 1933, President Roosevelt began his fireside chats.
He spoke to the nation in a calm voice.
Many people felt he was talking right to them.
Board games filled long evenings at the kitchen table.
Parker Brothers began selling Monopoly in 1935.
Players got rich on paper, while real wallets stayed thin.
Children invented games that cost nothing at all.
Kids rolled hoops, played marbles, and flew homemade kites.
Stickball and sandlot baseball ruled the summer streets.
Old socks were stuffed to make a ball.
Spools and scrap wood became toys.
A trip to the movies was a special treat.
For a small price, you got hours of escape.
Dishes and fancy glassware were sometimes given away at theaters.
Families treasured these small pleasures more than ever.
Now, here is the secret I promised.
The secret was other people, all along.
Neighbors traded eggs, vegetables, tools, and a helping hand.
A man might fix a roof for a basket of food.
Some towns even printed their own scrip to keep trade going.
Families doubled up, with relatives moving into one house.
Grandparents, cousins, and children shared the same roof.
Churches collected clothing and handed out meals.
Soup kitchens served hot food to people with no work.
Cities saw long lines of men waiting for a bowl.
Some people built shacks from scrap and called them home.
Those shantytowns were bitterly nicknamed Hoovervilles, after the president.
Children pitched in as soon as they were able.
Boys sold newspapers on street corners after school.
Girls helped with sewing, cooking, and younger siblings.
Some teenagers left school to find any paying work.
Every nickel they earned went into the family pot.
Then, in March 1933, Roosevelt took office.
He declared a bank holiday to stop panic withdrawals.
Soon after, the government created deposit insurance for bank accounts.
People could finally trust their savings again.
The New Deal brought a flood of new programs.
The Civilian Conservation Corps put young men to work outdoors.
They planted trees and built trails and park buildings.
Workers earned thirty dollars a month; twenty-five went home.
In 1935, the Works Progress Administration began hiring.
Over the years, it employed millions of Americans.
They built roads, bridges, schools, and playgrounds across the country.
That same year, Congress passed the Social Security Act.
It aimed to protect older people from poverty.
Still, the hard years lasted through the decade.
Those years left habits that never really faded.
Many survivors kept saving string, jars, and scraps.
They reused foil, mended clothes, and hated waste.
So how did a dollar last a week?
With beans, bread, gardens, patches, and endless patience.
With neighbors who shared, and children who helped.
It was never easy, but families held together.
